terminal.description: A shell that starts in the shop's top folder. Run each search and read what it prints before you save it.

tasks.title: Save the Pellow Bakery orders
tasks.description:
Save every line of `sales/web-orders.csv` that is an order from Pellow Bakery into `pellow-bakery.txt` in the top folder, each line as it is in the file. Pellow Farm Shop is a different customer, and its orders stay out.

Check compares `pellow-bakery.txt` with the Pellow Bakery lines of `sales/web-orders.csv`.
nextSteps: Search `sales/web-orders.csv` for `Pellow` and read what comes back.
Search for the bakery's whole name, space included.
Read the output: no line from the farm shop, and no file name in front of the lines.
hints: One word matches both customers. The bakery's whole name has a space in it.
Put the whole name in quotes so it reaches `grep` as one piece of text. Without them, the shell splits it into two.
Run `grep "Pellow Bakery" sales/web-orders.csv > pellow-bakery.txt` from the top folder.

videos.title: Searching files and folders with grep

tasks.title: Save every jam in the March log
tasks.description:
Hesper typed the press log in a hurry, and a jam is written `jam`, `Jam` or `JAM`. Save every line of `logs/press-mar.log` that contains the word jam in any letter case into `jams.txt` in the top folder.

Check compares `jams.txt` with the lines of the March log that contain jam, in any capitals.
nextSteps: Search the March log for `jam` and count the lines.
Open the log with `less` and type `/Jam` to see how else it was written. Press `q` to leave.
Add the option that ignores letter case.
hints: `grep` cares about capitals unless you tell it not to.
`-i` makes `grep` match the word in any letter case.
Run `grep -i jam logs/press-mar.log > jams.txt` from the top folder.

tasks.title: Count the unpaid orders
tasks.description:
The last column of `sales/web-orders.csv` says whether an order is `paid` or `unpaid`. Count how many orders are unpaid and save the number, and only the number, into `unpaid-count.txt` in the top folder.

Check reads the number in `unpaid-count.txt` and compares it with the unpaid orders in `sales/web-orders.csv`.
nextSteps: Search for the unpaid orders and look at a few of them.
Make sure the word you search for does not also match the paid orders.
Ask `grep` for a count instead of the lines.
Save the count with `>` and look at it with `cat`.
hints: One of the options in the lesson prints a number instead of lines.
`-c` counts the matching lines. `paid` is also inside `unpaid`, so search for the word that only unpaid orders have.
Run `grep -c unpaid sales/web-orders.csv > unpaid-count.txt` from the top folder.

tasks.title: Find every wrong address in the messages
tasks.description:
Customers wrote in about parcels sent to the wrong address. Search every file in `messages`, in all its folders, for the phrase `wrong address`, and save each line found, with its file's path and its line number in front, into `wrong-address.txt` in the top folder.

Check compares `wrong-address.txt` with every line in `messages` that contains wrong address: the path from the top folder, the line number and the line. The order does not matter.
nextSteps: Look at how `messages` is laid out with `ls messages`.
Search the whole folder for the phrase, with the option that goes into every folder.
Add the option that numbers lines, and read the output.
hints: Two options from the lesson are needed together: one walks the folders, one adds line numbers.
`-r` searches a folder and every folder in it, `-n` numbers the lines. Keep the phrase in quotes, and name `messages` as the place to search.
Run `grep -rn "wrong address" messages > wrong-address.txt` from the top folder.
